[ALUSI-FULL:v9p120#2/r9] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · أبو القاسم القشيري | reports | Those interpreting ilhad this way hold that God’s names are textually specified: only names established in the Qur’an, Sunnah, or consensus may be used.

[ALUSI-FULL:v9p121/r10] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | Depending on whether the issue is classified as practical, some treat a non-severely-weak report like a good report and analogy like consensus; others prohibit analogy, which the author calls the apparent position because synonyms can differ in implication.

[ALUSI-FULL:v9p121/r12] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | Names established by consensus include the Creator, the Existing, the Necessary, and the Eternal; some add the Cause, while others say the Creator and Eternal are transmitted names like al-Ḥannān and al-Mannān.
[ALUSI-FULL:v9p121/r13] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · بعض المحققين | reports | Some authorities forbid an unqualified form when it is an analogical synonym of a transmitted possessive form, and reject terms appearing only figuratively or by wordplay; verbs and verbal nouns alone do not authorize an adjective.

[ALUSI-FULL:v9p121/r18] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · بعض الناس | reports | Terms for meanings that are neither necessary nor impossible, such as scheming and deception, are usable only when revelation authorizes them; one must not invoke God as deceiver.

[TABATABAI:7:180-186#2/r3] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | The word al-malik with kasra and al-mulk with ḍamma both express God's absolute ownership and dominion, as many verses affirm.

[TABATABAI:7:180-186#4/r1] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | rejects | He rejects reducing knowledge, power, life, and all other attributes to mere negations, since that would deny every perfection and conflicts with natural disposition and Qur'anic wording.

[TABATABAI:7:180-186#4/r3] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | Attributes divide into positive perfections such as knowledge and life, and negative names such as al-Subbūḥ and al-Quddūs that express transcendence from defect.
[TABATABAI:7:180-186#4/r4] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | Active attributes such as creating and providing presuppose the essence and are derived from God's acts; unlike essential attributes, they are not intrinsic acquisitions.
[TABATABAI:7:180-186#4/r5] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | Attributes also divide into nonrelational self-attributes, self-attributes with an external relation, and purely relational attributes, such as life, creating, and being Creator or provider.
[TABATABAI:7:180-186#4/r6] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | A quality denotes a meaning attributed to the essence, while a name denotes the essence under a quality; life and knowledge are attributes, and living and knowing are names.
[TABATABAI:7:180-186#5/r1] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | People infer God's names from perfections observed in the world, because God owns and gives them; observed deficiencies show that He is free of them and possesses their opposite perfections.
[TABATABAI:7:180-186#5/r2] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | Divine attributes mediate between God and creation: His knowledge, power, provision, and beneficence supply creatures' corresponding needs and deficiencies.
[TABATABAI:7:180-186#5/r3] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | People fittingly invoke God by names suited to their needs: the one seeking wealth uses the Rich, Mighty, or Powerful, while the sick person calls on the Healer, Clement, or Merciful.
[TABATABAI:7:180-186#5/r4] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | The Qur'an validates this practice by ending passages with names suited to their meaning and using names to explain its claims; it is the only revealed scripture known to the author that teaches divine names.
[TABATABAI:7:180-186#5/r5] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | Creatures relate to God through His names and their widespread effects: manifestations of beauty and majesty connect them to those names, and the names connect them to the sustaining divine essence.

[TABATABAI:7:180-186#9/r2] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | rejects | There is no exegetical proof that divine names are restricted to transmitted forms; the opposing argument assumes both a covenantal reading of the article and that illicit naming means exceeding transmitted names, and both assumptions are questionable.

[TABATABAI:7:180-186/r1] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | These verses continue the preceding argument by restating that guidance and misguidance turn on calling God by His beautiful names or distorting them.
[TABATABAI:7:180-186/r2] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | By natural disposition, people agree that the visible world depends on God, who orders it, originates and receives all things, and gives it its beauty and perfection.
[TABATABAI:7:180-186/r3] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | One group names God only with attributes of perfection or names that negate every defect, thereby calling on Him by the beautiful names.
[TABATABAI:7:180-186/r4] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | A second group distorts divine names by assigning creation, life, or provision to matter or time, good to idols, divine prerogatives to prophets or saints, or independent power to created causes.
[TABATABAI:7:180-186/r5] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | A third group believes in God but attributes defects to Him, including body, location, sensory apprehension, humanlike knowledge, will, or power, temporal persistence, injustice, and ignorance.

[TABATABAI:7:180/r1] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | A name linguistically denotes an object, either with descriptive meaning or as a bare reference to the essence; the phrase beautiful names points to descriptive names, not bare proper names.
[TABATABAI:7:180/r2] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | Not every descriptive meaning is a beautiful name: a name must express the best perfection when considered with the divine essence, without inseparable deficiency.
[TABATABAI:7:180/r3] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | Courage and chastity are unsuitable divine names because they imply bodily particularity, whereas generosity, justice, and mercy can be purified of such limitation.
